about.lead: DiScammer is a field guide for anyone who has ever hesitated over a suspicious message and wondered if it was real. We describe how common scams work and let you practice on simulated situations. The point is not to finish a course. It is to build the reflex of pausing and checking.
about.title: Who we are, and why this exists.
about.what_we_believe_body: Specifics are what persuade: we name the SMS that pretends to come from a bank, the channel a romance scam can use, and the time-pressure phrase that should make you pause. Plain language beats jargon. The reader is an equal, not a target.
about.what_we_dont_do_item_1: No scare tactics. We don't exaggerate a danger to get you to click.
about.what_we_dont_do_item_2: The checkers analyze pasted text and links in the browser. Standard service and error logs can record technical request information needed to operate and protect the site; pasted inputs are not used for tracking.
about.what_we_dont_do_item_3: No partnerships with surveillance vendors. No affiliate links to identity-monitoring services.
about.what_we_dont_do_item_4: No paywall, no subscription, no "premium" tier. The lessons stay free.
about.what_we_do_item_1: Maintain a threat database of 10+ scam patterns with practical red flags and next steps.
about.what_we_do_item_2: Publish field briefings: interviews with analysts, newsletters, and long-form articles.
about.what_we_do_item_3: Run a self-guided nine-module course with a completion record stored in this browser, not a proctored or independently verified credential.
about.what_we_do_item_4: Offer a browser-based simulator with training scenarios based on common scam patterns.

portfolio.title: An education project designed to make the pause visible.
portfolio.lead: DiScammer is a bilingual anti-scam learning project. This dossier names its author, separates current implementation from future work, and records the decisions behind the public site.
portfolio.status_body: This is a public build record, not an external audit or an institutional credential. It describes the current website and its limits so a reviewer can distinguish implemented behavior from planned validation.
portfolio.author_body: DiScammer is a portfolio project by Foma Molchanov. The project does not claim an institutional partnership, a professional security audit, or external certification.
portfolio.problem_body: Fraud education often appears after a loss or as a generic warning. DiScammer turns recurring scam patterns into small, readable decisions: pause, identify the pressure, and verify through a channel you already trust.
portfolio.audience_body: The public site is written for Russian- and English-speaking adults who use email, messaging, marketplaces, or banking apps. It assumes no technical background and is designed for short sessions on a phone as well as longer study on a laptop.
portfolio.contribution_notice: This is a documented scope of the current project, not a signed personal contribution ledger. Foma should confirm the exact division of work before using it in an application.
portfolio.contribution_product_body: The current product connects guides, a course, interactive checkers, and a simulation around one intended behavior: taking a pause before acting on a suspicious request.
portfolio.contribution_engineering_body: The current site is a server-rendered FastAPI application with Jinja templates and React islands, a SQLite content layer, TypeScript components, and a production build pipeline.
portfolio.contribution_design_body: The Field Office visual system uses a restrained, reading-first interface where technical cues identify information rather than decorate it.
portfolio.contribution_privacy_body: The message and link checkers inspect pasted inputs in the browser. The site still has normal technical access and error logging, so the public copy does not describe the service as collecting no data at all.
portfolio.contribution_accessibility_body: The implementation includes authored Russian and English interfaces, semantic server-rendered pages, visible keyboard focus, a skip link, and reduced-motion support as product constraints rather than later add-ons.
portfolio.iteration_body: The current version moves the project beyond an earlier Tilda-based presentation toward a maintainable server-rendered application with focused client-side interactions. The aim of the revision is not more visual effects; it is a clearer explanation of what the project can and cannot promise.
portfolio.learning_1: A simulated analyst interface must never be mistaken for real operational authority.
portfolio.learning_2: A local completion record is a learning aid, not a proctored or independently verified credential.
portfolio.learning_3: Bilingual quality, accessible navigation, and input privacy need to be designed into the system, not translated or patched in later.
portfolio.validation_body: The codebase has automated checks for its backend, frontend, locale parity, and build process. DiScammer does not yet claim that users learn faster, lose less money, or change behavior after using it; no user-study result is presented as evidence.
portfolio.tools_body: The source toolchain includes Python, FastAPI, Jinja, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SQLite, Vite, and Docker. This is a technical inventory, not a statement about who used each tool.
portfolio.disclosure_body: The exact use of mentor feedback and AI-assisted tools must be confirmed by Foma before submission. This dossier does not present an automated tool, mentor, or external reviewer as an independent author, evaluator, or credential issuer.

guide.investigator_notes_fake_online_stores:
Educational pattern note, not a live investigation.
A convincing storefront, an unusually low price, and a rushed payment path can appear together.
A new or hidden domain record is a reason to slow down, not proof by itself.
Before ordering, find independent reviews and the retailer's contact details through a channel you choose.
recommend: search "{domain} reviews scam" and verify the site before paying.
guide.investigator_notes_generic:
Educational pattern note, not a live investigation.
A single sign rarely settles whether a message is safe. Look for pressure, an unusual payment route, or a request to move the conversation away from a trusted channel.
Scam patterns change, so treat this guide as a prompt to verify rather than a complete threat feed.
recommend: study the red flags in this dossier and practice the next step in the simulator.
guide.investigator_notes_investment_pyramids:
Educational pattern note, not financial advice.
A scheme may rely on money from new participants rather than a clear, regulated investment activity.
Guaranteed or unusually high returns, pressure to recruit, and vague documentation are warning signs to investigate.
Testimonials and polished dashboards are not independent evidence.
recommend: check the provider with the relevant financial regulator before any deposit.
guide.investigator_notes_nigerian_letters:
Educational pattern note, not a report about a region or a group of people.
Advance-fee scams can arrive through email, messaging apps, dating platforms, or social media.
The story usually promises a larger sum after a small fee, transfer, or request for personal details.
The claimed payout is the hook, not evidence that money exists.
recommend: never pay to unlock a larger sum; verify through an independent channel instead.
guide.investigator_notes_phishing:
Educational pattern note, not a live threat report.
Phishing commonly borrows a trusted brand, a time limit, and a link that asks you to sign in or share a code.
Sender names, addresses, and links can change quickly, so a familiar label is not proof.
Do not use a link or phone number from the message to verify it.
recommend: open the official app or type a known address yourself.
guide.sources_limit: These links support general safety guidance. They do not verify a particular message, account, or offer, and they are not a live threat feed.
guide.sources_unavailable: No source record is available for this guide yet. Read it as background, not as a live alert.
guide.check_intro: With JavaScript on, a short recall quiz appears here. Either way, ask yourself these before you move on:
guide.check_1: Name how this scam opens: the message, call, or offer that starts it.
guide.check_2: Say out loud the one detail that gives it away, even when everything else looks legitimate.
guide.check_3: Decide your next step in advance: who you'd contact through a channel you already trust, and what you would never do (pay a fee, share a code, follow the link).

sync.loss_warning: A lost code cannot be recovered. There is no email, no password and no reset: the server cannot tell whose data is whose, so it has nothing readable to give back. Lose the code and the synced copy is gone for good. Save it somewhere safe before you link.

sync.erase_hint: Erasing deletes the synced copy itself. Progress stays in this browser, but no other device will be able to pull it again.
sync.erase_confirm_question: Erase the synced copy from the server? This deletes it for every device, and the code will no longer open anything. Progress in this browser is kept.

q1.prompt: An email with your bank's exact logo says "Urgent Security Update: your account is locked" and links to a page to sign in and regain access. What's the safest move?
q1.opt_a: Click the link and sign in, since the logo and branding look right
q1.opt_b: Ignore the link, open the bank's app or type its address yourself, and check there
q1.opt_c: Reply to the email asking whether the message is genuine
q1.tell: Anyone can copy a logo. Urgency plus a sign-in link is the real giveaway, so reach the bank by a route you chose, not the one the email hands you.

q2.prompt: A message claiming to be from your bank asks you to confirm your card number and password by email. What does that tell you?
q2.opt_a: It's fine if the email address looks like the bank's
q2.opt_b: It's normal for a security check
q2.opt_c: It's a scam: banks don't ask for passwords or card numbers by email
q2.tell: A bank will never ask for your password or full card details by email, so the request itself is the giveaway, however official the sender's address looks.

q3.prompt: You've landed on a sign-in page from a link. Before you type anything, what actually tells you it's the real site?
q3.opt_a: The address starts with https:// and the domain is exactly the company's own
q3.opt_b: It has a padlock icon in the address bar
q3.opt_c: The page looks identical to the real site
q3.tell: Fake sites can copy the page and often get a padlock too, but they can't own the real domain, so read the address letter by letter before you type anything.

q1.prompt: A text says: "URGENT: suspicious transaction on your account. Verify now: [link]". What do you do?
q1.opt_a: Tap the link quickly to stop the transaction
q1.opt_b: Don't tap the link. Call the number on the back of your card to check
q1.opt_c: Reply STOP to cancel the transaction
q1.tell: A text like this only works if you hurry. Leave the link alone and call the bank on the number printed on your card, and the fake transaction goes away with the panic.

q2.prompt: A call shows your bank's real name and number on the screen. Can you trust it's really them?
q2.opt_a: No: caller ID can be spoofed to show any name or number
q2.opt_b: Yes, the number on the screen proves who is calling
q2.opt_c: Yes, as long as the agent knows your name
q2.tell: A familiar number on the screen proves nothing, because caller ID is easy to fake: if anything sensitive comes up, hang up and call the official number yourself.

q3.prompt: Your phone rings once from an unknown international number and stops. What's the risk if you call back?
q3.opt_a: Nothing: a missed call is harmless
q3.opt_b: You'll be charged a small standard fee
q3.opt_c: It could be a premium-rate number that charges a lot per minute
q3.tell: A single ring is bait: the callback goes to a premium-rate line that runs up your bill, so don't return calls from numbers you don't recognise.

q1.prompt: A new store advertises a sought-after designer bag at 70% off, accepts only bank transfer, and shows no tracking after you pay. What's most likely?
q1.opt_a: It's a fake store built to take the payment and vanish
q1.opt_b: It's a real outlet clearing old stock
q1.tell: A price too good to be true, a transfer you can't undo and no tracking add up to a fake store, and the discount is the bait.

q2.prompt: If a risky online purchase turns out to be a scam, what best helps you get your money back?
q2.opt_a: Pay by direct bank transfer so it clears fast
q2.opt_b: Pay with a card or a method that offers buyer protection
q2.tell: Card and protected-payment charges can usually be disputed, while bank transfers and crypto are built to be final, which is exactly why scammers ask for them.

q3.prompt: The site has a padlock and "https://" in the address. Does that mean it's a legitimate shop?
q3.opt_a: Yes, https means the shop is verified
q3.opt_b: Yes, a padlock guarantees your money is safe
q3.opt_c: No. https only encrypts the connection, and a scam site can have it too
q3.tell: A padlock only means the connection is encrypted, and scam shops get one too, so judge the seller by reviews, contact details, and payment options.

q1.prompt: Someone you met online has chatted warmly for two months, always has a reason not to meet, and now needs money for a work "emergency", promising to repay you. What's happening?
q1.opt_a: A genuine partner you should help out
q1.opt_b: A romance scam: the slow build-up was setting up the money request
q1.opt_c: Bad luck that will pass if you help just this once
q1.tell: Warm chat, endless reasons not to meet, then a sudden emergency and a promise to repay: that's the romance-scam script, and the relationship was the cover for the ask.

q2.prompt: What is the single clearest warning sign in an online relationship?
q2.opt_a: A request for money from someone you've never met in person
q2.opt_b: They send a lot of compliments
q2.tell: Compliments and distance turn up in plenty of honest relationships. Money is the hard line: if someone you've never met asks for it, stop and check before you do anything else.

q3.prompt: The profile photos look almost too perfect. How can you check whether they were taken from someone else?
q3.opt_a: Ask them to send more photos
q3.opt_b: Trust it if the photos are high quality
q3.opt_c: Run a reverse-image search on the photos to see if they appear under other names
q3.tell: Scammers reuse stolen photos on many profiles, so a reverse-image search can turn up the same face under other names. A match is a strong warning; no match proves nothing.

q1.prompt: An "investment" pays early members using money from newer members rather than from any real profit. What is that?
q1.tell: If the payouts come from new deposits rather than real earnings, it's a pyramid, and it stands only as long as new money keeps arriving.

q2.prompt: A scheme promises steady returns far above the market with "little to no risk". How should you read that?
q2.opt_a: A rare opportunity worth acting on fast
q2.opt_b: A fraud signal: guaranteed high returns with no risk don't exist
q2.tell: Higher returns mean higher risk, so big guaranteed profit with no risk is a pitch for something that doesn't exist.

q3.prompt: Your payout depends mainly on recruiting more people to join. What does that structure tell you?
q3.opt_c: It's a pyramid: real investments don't need a constant stream of new recruits
q3.tell: If you're paid mainly for recruiting rather than for a real product or profit, it's a pyramid, and it stops paying the moment recruiting slows.

q1.prompt: An offer says you can double your money fast, but only if you join today, because the spots are "limited". What's going on?
q1.opt_a: A real chance you'd regret missing
q1.opt_b: A get-rich-quick scam: huge returns plus artificial time pressure
q1.tell: Easy doubling plus a ticking clock is designed to keep you from thinking, and the deadline exists so that you won't check.

q2.prompt: Early on, some members do receive payouts, which makes the scheme look real. Where does that money come from?
q2.opt_a: From newer investors' deposits, not real profit
q2.tell: Those first payouts are bait, paid out of later joiners' money, and they build trust just before the organisers vanish with the pool.

q3.prompt: A platform can't clearly explain where its profits come from. What should you do?
q3.opt_a: Invest a small amount to test it
q3.opt_c: Treat the vagueness as a red flag and stay out
q3.tell: If they can't explain where the profit comes from, assume there isn't any. An honest investment can describe how it makes money.

q1.prompt: A stranger emails that they need your help moving a large fortune out of a country and offers to share it with you. What is this?
q1.opt_c: A bank error in your favour
q1.tell: A stranger who offers you a fortune for your help is the classic 419 advance-fee setup: the "reward" never arrives, only the requests for money do.

q2.prompt: To "release" the promised money, they ask you to first pay fees, taxes, or a bribe. What's the right response?
q2.opt_a: Pay the small fee to unlock the larger sum
q2.opt_b: Refuse: you never pay to receive money you were promised
q2.tell: A real transfer never makes you pay first to get paid: the fee is the scam itself, and once you pay one, another "obstacle" turns up.

q3.prompt: The sender backs up the story with official-looking documents, seals, and signatures. Does that make it real?
q3.opt_a: Yes, official documents prove the deal
q3.opt_c: No: seals and documents are trivial to fake and prove nothing
q3.tell: Forged letterheads, seals and signatures cost almost nothing, so they can't vouch for a stranger; the tell is still the fortune you never asked for.

q1.prompt: You get a message saying you've won a big prize in a lottery you never entered. How should you read it?
q1.opt_a: You probably forgot entering and really won
q1.opt_b: A scam: real lotteries don't contact people who never entered
q1.tell: You can't win a draw you never entered, so an unexpected "you won" is the opening line of a prize scam.

q2.prompt: To claim the "winnings", you're told to pay a processing fee or tax first. What would a real prize ask of you up front?
q2.opt_a: Nothing: never a fee or tax to release it
q2.tell: A real prize never costs you anything to receive, so an upfront "fee" or "tax" to release winnings is the scam itself.

q3.prompt: The message gives a phone number to call to claim your prize. How do you verify it safely?
q3.opt_a: Call the number in the message, because it's official
q3.opt_b: Reply with your details to speed it up
q3.opt_c: Find the organisation's contact details yourself, not the ones in the message
q3.tell: The contact details in the message lead straight back to the scammers, so check with the organisation through details you found yourself.

q1.prompt: After a disaster, a page shows heartbreaking photos, presses you to give right now, and takes only gift cards or crypto. What does that add up to?
q1.opt_a: It shows the signs of a fake charity
q1.opt_b: It's a fast, modern way real charities collect
q1.tell: Pressure to give now plus a payment method that can't be traced is the fake-charity pattern, while real charities let you take your time and offer ways to give that leave a record.

q2.prompt: Before donating to an organisation you don't know, what's the reliable check?
q2.opt_a: Trust it if the website looks polished
q2.opt_b: Look it up in an official charity register and confirm it's really listed
q2.opt_c: Donate a small amount first to test it
q2.tell: Anyone can build a slick website; an official register tells you whether the charity actually exists and is accountable.

q3.prompt: You ask how the donations are spent and get vague, evasive answers. What does that signal?
q3.opt_a: Normal: charities keep their finances private
q3.opt_b: It's fine if they sound sincere
q3.opt_c: A red flag: real charities publish reports and can say where money goes
q3.tell: Genuine charities publish reports and can say where the money goes, so dodging that question is a strong sign this one isn't real.

q1.prompt: A remote-job site offers $500 a week for easy typing, no experience needed, but you must first pay a $50 "registration fee" to see the jobs. What is this?
q1.opt_b: A work-from-home scam: you pay and the real work never appears
q1.tell: Charging you to see the "jobs" is the scam itself: the fee is what they sell, and the easy income never turns up.

q2.prompt: What does a legitimate employer never do when hiring you?
q2.opt_a: Charge you a fee to start working or to access listings
q2.tell: A real job pays you and doesn't charge you to start, so any upfront fee for training or access is the clearest sign of a scam.

q3.prompt: The "company" has no verifiable address, no phone, just an email that goes unanswered after you pay. What is that?
q3.opt_a: Normal for a small remote business
q3.opt_b: Fine as long as the website looks professional
q3.opt_c: A major warning sign: legitimate employers have verifiable contact details
q3.tell: A business you can't reach or check can disappear with your money, so a missing address and contact details count as a serious red flag.

analyzer.input_label: Paste the message you want to check
analyzer.placeholder: Paste the suspicious text, email, or SMS here.
analyzer.example: URGENT: This is your bank's security department. We noticed unauthorized access, and your account will be suspended. To avoid suspension, tell us the one-time code we just sent by SMS and confirm your identity via this link: bit.ly/verify-account
analyzer.privacy: The text you paste is analyzed in your browser and is not sent to the application. Standard technical access and error events may still be logged without the pasted text.
analyzer.disclaimer: This is a read, not a verdict. A clean result is not a guarantee, and a flagged one is not proof. Use it to decide whether to slow down and check.
analyzer.clean_body: No common red flags showed up in this text. That is not a guarantee. Scammers adapt, and a clean read just means none of the usual patterns matched. If something still feels off, verify through a channel you already trust.

analyzer.first60_1: Stop. Do not click any link, call any number in the message, or read out any code.
analyzer.first60_2: Verify on your own terms. Open the bank app or call the number on the back of your card, not the one you were given.
analyzer.first60_3: If money or a code was already shared, contact your bank now and ask to freeze the card or reverse the transfer.

flags.urgency_body: It pushes you to act right now. Real institutions give you time. Pressure to move fast is meant to stop you from thinking.
flags.otp_ask_body: A code from an SMS or app is the key to your account. No real bank or service will ever ask you to read it out. Anyone who does is trying to get in.
flags.credential_ask_label: Asks for a password, PIN, or CVV
flags.credential_ask_body: Real staff never need your password, PIN, full card number, or CVV. Anyone who asks for them is trying to get at your money or your account.
flags.safe_account_body: There is no such thing as a safe or reserve account you move money to for protection. That phrase is a scam script, almost word for word.
flags.impersonation_body: It poses as your bank's security team, the police, a court, or your boss. The badge is borrowed to make you comply before you check.
flags.crypto_rail_body: Payment in Bitcoin, USDT, or any crypto wallet is irreversible and hard to trace. That is exactly why scammers prefer it.
flags.gift_card_rail_body: No real bill, fine, or fee is ever paid with iTunes, Google Play, or Steam cards. A gift-card request is a tell, every time.
flags.p2p_transfer_label: Wants a card or wire transfer
flags.p2p_transfer_body: Western Union, MoneyGram, or a transfer to someone's card is hard to claw back. Once it lands, the money is usually gone.
flags.url_shortener_body: A shortened link (bit.ly and the like) conceals where it actually goes. Expand it before you trust it, or do not open it at all.
flags.punycode_body: An address starting with xn-- uses encoded non-Latin letters. That can make it look like a familiar brand while it points somewhere else entirely.
flags.homograph_body: A word or domain mixes letters from two alphabets (for example a Cyrillic letter in place of a Latin one). That is a common way to imitate a name you trust.
flags.prize_win_body: You cannot win a lottery you never entered. A surprise prize is the hook, and the fee or details they ask for next is the catch.
flags.guaranteed_roi_body: No real investment can guarantee a big return on a schedule. Guaranteed profit is a classic sign of a pyramid or Ponzi scheme.
flags.qr_code_label: Asks you to scan a QR code
flags.qr_code_body: A QR code hides its destination behind an image. Scanning one can open a fake login page or trigger a payment. Treat it like any unknown link.
flags.deadline_clock_body: A countdown (within the hour, before midnight, expires today) is manufactured pressure. A real deadline survives you taking a day to verify.
flags.secrecy_label: Asks you to keep it secret
flags.secrecy_body: Being told not to mention it to your bank or family cuts you off from the people most likely to spot the con. Secrecy only helps the scammer.
flags.account_threat_body: A threat to suspend or freeze your account is meant to panic you into acting. Verify directly with the service before you touch anything.
flags.login_link_bait_label: Pushes you to log in via a link
flags.login_link_bait_body: It wants you to sign in or confirm details through a link it provides. That link can lead to a clone built to capture what you type. Go to the site yourself instead.
flags.advance_fee_label: Asks for a fee to release money
flags.advance_fee_body: Paying a small fee to release a much larger sum is the whole scam. The big sum does not exist; only the fees you keep paying do.
flags.attachment_bait_body: An invoice or document you did not expect can carry malware or a phishing page. Confirm with the sender through another channel before opening it.
flags.romance_money_body: Warmth from someone you have not met in person, followed by a request for money or help, is a classic pattern in pig-butchering and romance scams.

incident.disclosure: If you may already have shared or done something
incident.heading: Choose only what applies
incident.intro: This is an educational tool that runs on this page. It does not file a report, check what happened, or guarantee an outcome.
incident.privacy: Do not enter passwords, full card numbers, or recovery codes. Your choices stay on this page, and the tool does not ask you to send the message or link to DiScammer.
incident.impact_money: I sent money or approved a payment
incident.impact_credentials: I shared a password or one-time code
incident.impact_device: I installed an app or gave remote access
incident.impact_identity: I shared identity or account details
incident.impact_received_only: I only received a suspicious message
incident.action_stop: Pause contact and do not send another payment, code, or document.
incident.action_trusted_channel: Open the official app or type the official site yourself. Use a number from a card, statement, or verified website, not from the message.
incident.action_money: If money moved or a payment was approved, contact the bank or payment provider through that trusted channel as soon as you can. Ask what options apply; no result is guaranteed.
incident.action_credentials: If you shared a password or code, change the password from a device you trust, review sign-in sessions, and enable multi-factor authentication where available. Contact the provider through its official route.
incident.action_device: If you installed an app or gave remote access, end the session. Use only the device maker's or service provider's official guidance before changing anything else.
incident.action_identity: If you shared identity or account details, contact the relevant provider through an official channel and ask which protective steps apply where you live.
incident.action_tell_trusted: Tell someone you trust what happened, especially before making another decision alone.
incident.immediate_danger: If someone is pressuring you in person or you feel unsafe, move to a safer place and contact the emergency service available where you are.

inspect.input_label: Paste the link you want to inspect
inspect.placeholder: Paste the suspicious link here. It is not opened.
inspect.privacy: The link you paste is analyzed in your browser. It is not sent to the application or opened by it; standard technical access and error events may still be logged without the pasted link.
inspect.disclaimer: This is a rough read of the address alone, not a verdict on the site. A clean read is not a guarantee, and a flagged one is not proof. Use it to decide whether to slow down.
inspect.clean_body: None of the usual link tells showed up in this address. That is not a guarantee: a page can still be fake behind a clean-looking link. If something feels off, type the address yourself or open an app you already trust.
inspect.empty_prompt: Paste a link and press INSPECT, or load an example to see how it works.

explain.punycode_body: A part of the host starts with xn--, the encoding browsers use for non-Latin letters. It can render as a familiar name while pointing somewhere else entirely.
explain.homograph_body: The host mixes alphabets, for example a Cyrillic а in place of a Latin a. That is a common way to pass for a name you trust at a glance.
explain.ip_host_label: Raw IP address instead of a name
explain.ip_host_body: The host is a bare number like 192.168.0.1, not a domain name. Real services use named domains; a raw IP hides who actually owns the address.
explain.userinfo_trick_body: There is an @ in the address. The browser ignores everything before it and goes to whatever follows the @, so bank.com@evil.ru actually goes to evil.ru.
explain.deceptive_subdomain_label: Trusted name used as a sub-domain
explain.deceptive_subdomain_body: A known brand name appears at the front of the host, but a prefix says nothing about who controls the site. Domain endings vary in length (.com, .co.uk), so this is a cautious rule of thumb, not a check of who owns the domain.
explain.brand_lookalike_body: The domain is one or two characters off a brand you know: a swapped letter, or a digit posing as one (paypa1, g00gle). It is made to pass a quick glance.
explain.suspicious_tld_body: The address ends in a domain extension scammers lean on heavily (like .zip or .top). It is not proof on its own, but it is worth a second look.
explain.shortener_label: Shortened link hides the real address
explain.shortener_body: A shortener (bit.ly and the like) conceals where the link actually goes. Expand it first, or do not open it at all.
explain.not_https_body: The address is http, not https, so the connection is not encrypted. Login and payment pages should use HTTPS, but HTTPS alone does not prove a site is authentic.
explain.port_oddity_body: The address names an unusual port (the number after a colon, like :8080). Ordinary sites do not need one, and it can point to a service set up to imitate a real one.
explain.obfuscated_path_body: The part after the host is unusually long or packed with encoded characters. That is often used to bury the real destination or slip extra parameters past a quick look.

check.heading: Check a message before you act on it.
check.lead: Paste a message that feels off and see which known scam patterns it matches. It is a quick read, meant to give you a pause: a few seconds between the message and your reaction, enough for a second look.
check.how_1: Paste the full message: the SMS, email, or chat text, links and all.
check.how_2: Press ANALYZE. The check runs in your browser and shows which red flags stood out.
check.how_3: Treat any flag as a reason to slow down and verify through a channel you already trust, not as a final verdict.
check.privacy_body: The analyzer reads pasted text in your browser and does not send that text to the application. Standard technical access and error events may still be logged without the pasted content. The analysis itself can run without an internet connection.
check.example_intro: Here is an invented message of the kind scammers send, and the flags it trips, to show what the check looks for:
check.example_message: Sberbank Security: an unauthorized login to your account was detected. To avoid suspension, confirm your identity via the link bit.ly/sber-verify and tell us the one-time code we just sent by SMS. Do this within 15 minutes. Do not tell anyone, including bank staff.
check.example_flag_1: Claims to be bank security (borrowed authority).
check.example_flag_2: Threatens to suspend the account and sets a 15-minute deadline (manufactured panic).
check.example_flag_3: Hides the link behind a shortener and pushes you to 'confirm your identity' through it.
check.example_flag_4: Asks for the one-time code from SMS, which no real bank ever does.
check.example_flag_5: Tells you to keep it secret, even from bank staff, to remove anyone who might stop you.
check.incident_intro: Start with a pause. These general steps are for education and do not report, verify, or resolve an incident.
check.incident_1: Stop communicating and do not send another payment, code, or document.
check.incident_2: Use a contact route you find yourself: the official app, a typed address, or a number from your card or statement.
check.incident_3: If a payment was approved or money moved, contact the bank or payment provider through that trusted channel and ask what options are available.
check.incident_4: If you shared a password or code, change it from a device you trust, review sign-in sessions, and use multi-factor authentication where available.
check.incident_5: If you installed an app, gave remote access, or shared account or identity details, end the session and follow only official provider or device-maker guidance.
check.incident_6: Tell someone you trust before you make another decision alone.
check.incident_privacy: These general steps do not require you to paste or send a message, link, password, card number, or recovery code.
check.incident_disclaimer: Educational guidance only. This page cannot file a report, verify an incident, recover funds, or guarantee an outcome.
check.incident_danger: If someone is pressuring you in person or you feel unsafe, move to a safer place and contact emergency services where you are.
check.noscript_intro: JavaScript is off, so the live analyzer is unavailable. Run this checklist by hand on any suspicious message:
check.noscript_1: Does it pressure you to act immediately or set a countdown? Real deadlines usually survive a day's delay.
check.noscript_2: Does it ask for a one-time code, password, PIN, or CVV? No legitimate service ever will.
check.noscript_3: Does it ask you to move money to a 'safe account' or pay a fee to release a larger sum? Both are classic scam moves.
check.noscript_4: Does it want crypto, gift cards, or a wire transfer? These are chosen because they are hard to reverse.
check.noscript_5: Does the link hide its real destination (a shortener, or odd lookalike characters)? Do not click it.
check.noscript_6: Does it tell you to keep it secret? Secrecy protects the scammer. Verify through a channel you already trust.

inspect.heading: Inspect a link before you click
inspect.lead: A bad link is one of the most common ways a scam reaches you. Paste a web address and the inspector takes it apart in your browser, naming each tell and pointing you to the phishing guide. It reads the address itself and does not open it.
inspect.how_1: Copy the link without opening it. On a phone, press and hold; on a computer, right-click and copy the link address.
inspect.how_2: Paste it into the box and press INSPECT. The inspector reads the address, not the page behind it.
inspect.how_3: Read the tells. Each one explains what it found and why it matters. When in doubt, type the real address yourself instead of clicking.
inspect.privacy_body: The inspector reads the pasted link in your browser. It does not upload or open the link, though standard technical access and error events may still be logged without the pasted address. This is a heuristic read of the address, not a verdict on the site.
inspect.example_intro: Here is an address that looks almost right, and exactly where it goes wrong.
inspect.example_flag_1: In this .ru example, the address belongs to secure-login.ru, not paypal.com. The paypal.com part is just a prefix, not the destination. Endings differ from domain to domain, so counting a fixed number of parts will not always find the real domain.
inspect.example_flag_2: It starts with http, not https, so the connection is not encrypted. Login and payment pages should use HTTPS, but HTTPS alone does not prove a site is authentic.
inspect.example_flag_3: A trusted brand name is bolted onto an unrelated domain to win a moment of trust at a glance. Read the host from the right, and verify through a channel you already trust if it matters.
inspect.noscript_heading: HOW TO READ A LINK BY HAND
inspect.noscript_intro: The inspector needs JavaScript. Without it, here is the same checklist you can run on any link in your head.
inspect.noscript_1: Find the real domain. Read the host from the right, and do not assume a fixed number of parts: endings differ, for example .com and .co.uk. If it matters, verify through a channel you already trust.
inspect.noscript_2: Watch for a brand bolted onto another domain, like paypal.com.secure-login.ru. The link really goes to secure-login.ru.
inspect.noscript_3: Be wary of an @ in the address. Anything before it is ignored by the browser; the real host is what follows the @.
inspect.noscript_4: Distrust raw numbers for a host (like 192.168.0.1) and links that start with http instead of https.
inspect.noscript_5: Look hard at lookalikes: a digit standing in for a letter (paypa1), or a foreign letter that mimics a Latin one (Cyrillic а for a).
inspect.noscript_6: When anything looks off, do not click. Type the address you know yourself, or open the app you already trust.
inspect.incident_heading: If you already opened the link
inspect.incident_intro: Pause first. These general steps are educational: they do not confirm an incident, file a report, or repair an account.
inspect.incident_1: If you only opened or clicked the link, stop interacting. Do not enter new information, approve a prompt, or follow another link from the page.
inspect.incident_2: Reach the service another way: use its official app, type the address you already know, or use a contact detail from your card or statement.
inspect.incident_3: If you entered a password, one-time code, card detail, or recovery code, use the trusted route to change or protect the affected account. Follow the provider's official guidance.
inspect.incident_4: If you confirmed a payment or sent money, contact your bank or payment provider through that trusted route and ask what options are available.
inspect.incident_5: If a file downloaded or an app installed, do not open it. Follow security guidance from your device maker, your operating-system provider, or the service you use.
inspect.incident_6: Tell someone you trust before the next decision. You do not need to share sensitive details with this page.
inspect.incident_privacy: These steps do not need the link, the page, a password, a card number, a one-time code, or a downloaded file.
inspect.incident_disclaimer: Educational guidance only. This page cannot file a report, verify an incident, recover funds, or guarantee an outcome.
inspect.incident_danger: If someone is pressuring you in person or you feel unsafe, move to a safer place and contact emergency services where you are.

analytics.heading: Visit analytics
analytics.notice: We use Umami to measure public page views and a few actions, such as opening the game or marking a lesson complete. Pasted messages, inspected links, search text and form values are not sent. We do not use analytics cookies or session recordings.
analytics.network: Umami receives normal network information (including your IP address and browser information) to estimate location and group visits. We send only the referring website’s origin. We respect Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control.
analytics.disabled: Analytics is disabled in this browser.
